strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly demonstrates (Fig. 1, leave-one-out experiment) that static caching schedules are suboptimal across rollout iterations, providing strong empirical justification for a rollout-adaptive approach.

The proposed pruner architecture is lightweight (parameter- and inference-efficient, <0.3% FLOPs overhead) and predicts a global sparsity pattern in a single forward pass, which is a sensible engineering solution to avoid negating speedup gains.

The 'one-for-all' cross-block/cross-timestep reuse strategy is a novel and reasonably well-motivated extension over prior block-wise or purely temporal caching schemes, backed by an activation-similarity analysis (Fig. 4a, Appendix A.7).

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple RoboMimic tasks (PH/MH), the multi-stage Kitchen benchmark, and a real-world Franka pick-and-release task, compared against a good spread of relevant baselines (DDIM, EfficientVLA, BAC, Falcon, SDP, CP, L2C).
Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of the real-time pruner, the one-for-all reusing strategy, and the global sparsity loss, showing each component is important.
Additional analyses (pruning-rate stability, loss curves, sinusoidal encoding ablation, sparsity-pattern visualizations) support reproducibility and give insight into the method's behavior.
weaknesses: The pruner is trained per-task using a reference dataset with a fidelity loss against a frozen policy; this requires task-specific training/fine-tuning of a new network for every deployment scenario, which is a nontrivial practical limitation compared to training-free caching baselines (e.g., BAC, EfficientVLA) but is not clearly discussed as such in the paper.

It is unclear how the pruner can predict the entire K×3L sparsity mask from only the current observation before any denoising has begun, given that the model's internal computation/redundancy pattern could also depend on the specific noise realization and intermediate states, not just ot. This design choice needs more justification or ablation to substantiate that observation alone is sufficient information.

The claim of 'lossless' acceleration is undercut by results where SAG's success rate exceeds the Full Precision baseline (e.g., Square PH 89% vs 88%, Transport PH 85% vs 78%, several MH tasks), which is unusual for a pure computation-pruning method and suggests the fidelity-loss fine-tuning stage may be altering behavior beyond simple speedup; this effect is not analyzed or explained.

No comparison of the additional training cost (wall-clock time, data collection effort for Dref, hyperparameter tuning across weight-decay settings) relative to training-free caching baselines, which would be important for assessing overall practicality.
Some notation is imprecise/hard to parse (e.g., the floor(b/3) indexing in Eq. 12 combined with the block-group description), which could hinder reproducibility.

The paper does not discuss what happens when the environment or task distribution shifts from the training distribution used to fit the pruner, i.e., generalization/robustness of the learned pruner is not evaluated.

Limitations section is essentially absent from the main text; risks such as task-specific retraining requirements, sensitivity to the pruning-rate hyperparameter, and behavior under distribution shift are not explicitly acknowledged.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem (Diffusion Policy inference latency) and provides a clear, well-motivated empirical observation (Fig. 1, leave-one-out schedule evaluation) showing that fixed caching schedules are suboptimal across rollout iterations, which is a reasonable and interesting motivation for an adaptive approach.

The proposed architecture for the pruner is lightweight by design (claimed <0.3% FLOPs overhead), and the idea of conditioning pruning decisions on the current observation rather than relying on post-hoc activation profiling is a sensible way to avoid the chicken-and-egg problem of rule-based caching.

The one-for-all reusing strategy, which exploits observed cross-block similarity (Fig. 4a) in addition to cross-timestep similarity, is a reasonable extension beyond the block-local caching paradigm used by prior caching methods such as BAC and EfficientVLA.

The empirical evaluation spans multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboMimic PH/MH, multi-stage Kitchen task) and includes a real-world robot experiment, along with a reasonably thorough set of ablations isolating the contribution of the pruner, the reusing strategy, and the sparsity loss.
The paper is transparent about using an LLM only for polishing and provides some supplementary material on pruning-rate stability and loss curves.
weaknesses: Fairness of the comparison is questionable: SAG requires training a task-specific pruner supervised with ground-truth actions on an additional reference subset (5% of the original training data) for each task, whereas most baselines (e.g., EfficientVLA, BAC, Falcon) are training-free. This learned, per-task-tuned nature of SAG is not clearly acknowledged as a limitation, and the comparison table does not control for this extra training cost or data access, which undermines the claimed superiority.

The central motivating claim in the introduction is that Diffusion Policy needs 50-1000Hz control frequency, yet the real-world result (Fig. 5) shows SAG only achieves ~40.5Hz, which is still well below the stated requirement for a Franka arm; this gap between the motivating claim and the demonstrated result is not addressed or discussed.

Several results labeled as 'lossless' acceleration are inconsistent with the actual numbers: e.g., in Table 1, SAG's success rate on Tool is 50% vs. 51% for Full Precision, and in Table 2, Transport MH is 50% vs. 54% for Full Precision — these are losses, not lossless gains, yet the abstract and conclusion uniformly claim 'lossless' 4x acceleration without qualification or statistical significance testing (only mean ± std is reported, no significance tests).

Several success-rate improvements over Full Precision (e.g., Transport PH: 85% vs. 78%; Square MH: 79% vs. 76%) are notable and somewhat suspicious for a pruned/accelerated model to systematically outperform its unpruned counterpart; this phenomenon is not explained mechanistically (e.g., as regularization effect) nor validated with more rigorous statistical analysis, raising concerns about cherry-picked seeds or insufficient trial counts.

The ablation study reveals that removing the global sparsity loss causes catastrophic collapse (success rates dropping to 0% on several tasks), indicating that the training procedure is highly brittle and sensitive to this specific loss design; this fragility is not discussed as a limitation, and no sensitivity analysis of the pruning-rate hyperparameter ρ (fixed at 91% across all tasks regardless of task difficulty) is provided.

The real-world evaluation is limited to a single, relatively simple pick-and-release task with modest success rates (54%), which is not strong evidence of generalization or robustness in realistic deployment settings; broader real-world validation across more diverse manipulation tasks would strengthen the significance claim.

No explicit Limitations section is included; known weaknesses such as task-specific retraining requirements, pruner data/label dependency, and the gap to true real-time frequency requirements are not candidly discussed.
The project page link is left as a placeholder, and no code repository is referenced, which raises concerns about reproducibility beyond the implementation details given in the appendix.

The notation in the methodology (e.g., overloading the block index b across Eq. 12-13, use of ⌊b/3⌋ for layer indexing) is somewhat unclear and could benefit from a cleaner, more explicit formalization connecting the block/timestep grouping to the shared buffer mechanism.

strengths: Well-motivated central observation: the leave-one-out experiment in Figure 1 convincingly demonstrates that fixed caching/pruning schedules used by prior work are suboptimal across rollout iterations, providing clear empirical justification for the proposed adaptive approach.

Thorough and broad empirical evaluation across multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboMimic PH/MH on five tasks, multi-stage Kitchen) and a real-world Franka pick-and-release task, compared against a comprehensive set of strong, representative baselines (DDIM, EfficientVLA, BAC, L2C, Falcon, SDP, CP).

Detailed ablation studies isolate the contribution of each proposed component (real-time pruner, one-for-all reusing, global sparsity loss), showing each is important, with especially dramatic effects from the global sparsity loss.

The proposed pruner is lightweight (claimed <0.3% FLOPs overhead) and operates with a single forward pass, which is a sensible engineering solution to avoid negating speedup gains from the pruning mechanism itself.

Good supplementary analysis in the appendix, including pruning-rate stability over rollouts, training/validation loss curves across different sparsity budgets, redundancy visualizations motivating the one-for-all reuse strategy, and ablation on positional encoding design choices.
The paper clearly decomposes the inference pipeline into rollout/denoising/block levels, which gives a clean conceptual framework for identifying and exploiting different forms of redundancy.
weaknesses: The claim of 'lossless' acceleration is somewhat overstated given that success rate differences between SAG and the full-precision baseline are often within or close to the reported standard deviations (e.g., Square: 88±7.0 vs 89±2.5; Transport: 78±3.3 vs 85±3.3), and no statistical significance testing is provided across the limited number of seeds, making it hard to confirm 'lossless' or 'performance gain' claims rigorously.

The pruner requires task-specific supervised training using a reference dataset drawn from the same distribution as the training data (5% of training set) for each task; this undercuts the framing of SAG as purely 'real-time' and 'environment-aware' since it still requires an offline, task-specific training phase, and the paper does not discuss how well the learned pruner generalizes to novel initial conditions, object configurations, or distribution shift within a task, nor across tasks.

The ablation of the global sparsity loss compares against a uniform block-wise budget, which may be a relatively weak strawman that is known a priori to ignore block importance; the dramatic collapse to 0% success in some tasks might partly reflect the fact that this alternative is a naive baseline rather than fully isolating the specific design choice.

Real-world validation is limited to a single manipulation task (pick-and-release) with modest absolute success rates (54%), making it difficult to assess robustness and generalizability of the approach under more diverse and higher-precision real-world conditions.

The paper does not report the additional training cost (wall-clock time, compute) required to train the per-task diffusion pruner, which is relevant for assessing the practicality and reproducibility of the method, especially as it needs to be retrained whenever the base policy or task changes.

Presentation is at times dense with heavy notation (e.g., the block/timestep grouping and gating formalism in Sec 2.2–2.3), and could benefit from a higher-level explanation or more intuitive illustration of how the mask and reuse mechanism interact during inference beyond the pseudocode.

Some very recent and closely related work in the same research direction (e.g., temporal-adaptive diffusion policy acceleration methods cited in the reference list) is not directly compared against, even if only mentioned, leaving open how SAG differentiates from or improves upon concurrent efforts targeting similar rollout-dynamics-aware acceleration.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and well-motivated limitation of prior caching-based Diffusion Policy acceleration methods (fixed schedules) via a convincing leave-one-out empirical analysis (Fig. 1), which strongly justifies the need for rollout-adaptive pruning.

The proposed method is technically coherent: an observation-conditioned, lightweight pruner combined with a 'one-for-all' cross-block/cross-timestep reuse strategy is a sensible way to exploit the redundancy patterns shown empirically in Figure 4a and Appendix A.8.

Extensive experiments across multiple RoboMimic tasks (PH/MH), the multi-stage Kitchen benchmark, and real-world Franka Research 3 experiments, with comparisons to numerous strong baselines (EfficientVLA, BAC, DDIM, L2C, Falcon, SDP, CP), lend good empirical breadth to the claims.

Thorough ablation studies (pruner, reusing strategy, sparsity loss), sensitivity analysis on pruning rate, compatibility with DPM-Solver++, compute-matched comparisons with Consistency Policy, and robustness analyses (Appendix A.10-A.11) demonstrate a level of rigor and self-scrutiny that strengthens confidence in the results.

Real-time overhead of the pruner appears genuinely small, and the method achieves substantial (~3.6-4x) speedups while largely preserving or even improving task success rates, which is a meaningful practical contribution for real-time robot control.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: it combines existing ideas (learned/conditioned pruning masks via STE, akin to prior differentiable pruning approaches like DiP-GO, and cross-block/timestep caching) into a new architecture for the specific Diffusion Policy setting; the conceptual leap over related work (e.g., BAC, L2C, DiP-GO) is evolutionary rather than fundamentally novel.

Evaluation is limited to a single base policy (DP-T, transformer-based Diffusion Policy) and relatively simple RoboMimic/Kitchen tasks; the paper explicitly acknowledges this scope limitation, but it leaves open how well SAG would generalize to larger VLA-scale diffusion action experts (e.g., pi_0, RDT-1B) mentioned as key motivating use cases in the introduction, which is a significant gap given the framing around VLA models.

The reference dataset used to train/supervise the pruner (Dref, ~5% of training data) is drawn from the same distribution as training demonstrations; there is limited analysis of how the pruner generalizes to out-of-distribution rollout states or corrective/recovery behaviors that were not present in the small reference set, despite the paper's own recognition that the sparsity pattern should reflect visuomotor dynamics.

Some result inconsistencies and thin explanations: e.g., Table 6 ablation shows 'w/o Real-time Diffusion Pruner' average 83 vs SAG's 87 (a modest gap), whereas the text claims dropping this component leads to a decrease from '89%' — the specific numbers quoted in the text (e.g., 89% to 83%) do not exactly match the tables, raising minor concerns about consistency/reporting accuracy.

The paper claims 'without sacrificing performance' and reports performance *gains* over Full Computation in several tables (e.g., SAG outperforms Full Computation on Square/Transport), which is a bit suspicious for a pruning method and is not clearly explained (e.g., whether this is regularization effect, variance, or reference-dataset distillation-like effect); the paper does not adequately discuss why pruning would improve success rate beyond noting comparable performance.

The real-world evaluation is fairly small in scope (3 tasks, unspecified number of trials, Table 4) and does not report variance/confidence intervals unlike the simulation tables, making it harder to assess the statistical significance of the real-robot results.

The paper's approach requires training a separate task-specific pruner per task/policy with its own reference data and hyperparameters (target pruning rate ρ is manually set and tuned per deployment), which adds practical overhead and reduces the plug-and-play nature suggested in the abstract; the sensitivity analysis (Table 7) shows performance is highly sensitive to this hyperparameter (steep drop from 85% avg at 91% pruning to 51% at 97%), suggesting fragility that could complicate deployment in truly extreme sparsity or novel environments.

strengths: The motivating analysis (Fig. 1, leave-one-out evaluation of fixed caching schedules) is a clear and convincing empirical demonstration that static caching schedules are suboptimal across rollout iterations, providing good justification for the proposed approach.

The experimental scope is broad: multiple RoboMimic tasks (PH/MH), the multi-stage Kitchen benchmark, and three real-world Franka tasks, compared against a reasonably comprehensive set of baselines (DDIM, EfficientVLA, L2C, BAC, Falcon, SDP, CP).

The ablation study (Table 6) isolates the contribution of each proposed component (real-time pruner, one-for-all reusing, global sparsity loss) and shows each contributes measurably to final performance.

Additional appendix analyses (pruning-rate stability, loss curves, compute-matched comparison with Consistency Policy, block participation, redundancy visualizations) show an effort toward thorough empirical characterization.

The idea of conditioning a lightweight pruner on observations to predict a global (cross-block, cross-timestep) sparsity pattern in a single forward pass is a reasonable, well-motivated engineering solution to the stated problem.
weaknesses: Claimed '>90% computation pruned' coexists with only ~3.6-4x wall-clock speedup (Table 9), a substantial gap that is never explained (e.g., fixed overheads from the observation/vision encoder, pruner inference cost, or non-prunable components). Without a breakdown of where the remaining latency goes, the headline efficiency claims are not fully substantiated.

The real-time pruner is trained per task using a reference dataset Dref sampled from that task's demonstrations together with ground-truth actions and a policy-fidelity distillation loss (Eq. 9, Appendix A.3). This means SAG is not a plug-and-play, training-free accelerator for novel environments as the framing suggests ('without updating the model parameters' refers only to the base policy); the pruner itself must be retrained per task/robot, which is a significant and under-emphasized limitation not clearly surfaced in Sec. 5.

Reported gains over the strongest baseline (BAC) are often marginal or mixed at the per-task level (e.g., Can 98 vs 94, Square 89 vs 87, Tool 50 vs 51 where BAC is actually equal/better), while the paper's narrative of 'average performance gain of 13%/29%' is driven largely by other baselines' catastrophic failures (e.g., EfficientVLA collapsing on Kitchen), which can give a misleading impression of SAG's relative advantage over the most competitive alternative.

Real-world evaluation is limited (3 tasks) and the main results table (Table 4) does not report the number of trials or variance/confidence intervals, unlike the simulation tables; Fig. 5 bar charts also lack error bars, making it hard to assess the reliability of real-world success-rate differences (e.g., 26%→58% on Assembly Line).

The method's technical novelty is incremental: it combines known ingredients (learned/observation-conditioned scheduling akin to L2C/DiP-GO-style learned pruners, STE-based differentiable masking, cross-block/cross-timestep caching) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the distinction from existing block-wise adaptive caching work (BAC) is mainly the addition of observation conditioning and a global (vs. block-local) sparsity/reuse formulation, which is a reasonable but modest conceptual step.

Some experimental design choices appear favorable to SAG without clear justification of fairness, e.g., DPM-Solver++ comparison in Table 5 and compute-matched comparison with CP in Appendix A.5 use different operationalizations of 'equivalent budget' that are not rigorously cross-validated against the main-text metrics.

Minor concerns: an apparently self-dated future reference ('Ji et al., 2026', arXiv ID 2605.13316) appears in the bibliography, raising questions about citation accuracy; reproducibility is also not fully supported since no code repository link is provided (only a placeholder project page), and several architecture/training details (visual encoder choice, exact Transformer encoder depth/width of the pruner) are not fully specified in the main text.

strengths: The paper provides compelling empirical motivation (Fig. 1, leave-one-out schedule analysis) that clearly demonstrates the failure mode of static caching schedules across rollout iterations, which directly motivates the proposed adaptive approach.

Extensive experimental validation across multiple RoboMimic tasks (PH/MH), the multi-stage Kitchen benchmark, and three real-world Franka tasks, with consistent 3.4-4x speedups while matching or exceeding Full Computation baselines in several cases.

Thorough ablation studies (Table 6) isolating the contribution of each component (real-time pruner, one-for-all reusing, global sparsity loss), showing each is non-trivially important, with the removal of the global sparsity loss causing severe performance collapse that is honestly reported.

The one-for-all reusing strategy is a reasonably well-motivated architectural insight, backed by an empirical observation of cross-block activation similarity (Fig. 4a), that distinguishes this work from prior block-local caching schemes.

Good engineering care toward minimizing pruner overhead (single-pass, shared network across blocks/timesteps, sinusoidal positional encoding ablation in Fig. 3), and reporting of real-time pruning-rate stability (Appendix A.2) and latency breakdown (Appendix A.6), supporting reproducibility.
Supplementary robustness, sensitivity, and compute-matched comparisons (Appendices A.5, A.10, A.11) add good evidentiary depth beyond the main results.
weaknesses: The pruner requires supervised training per task using ground-truth action labels and a reference dataset (5% of training data), which is a meaningfully different setting from the training-free caching baselines it is compared against; this difference in requirement/assumption is not clearly flagged as a fairness caveat in the main comparison tables.

It is unclear whether a single pruner generalizes across tasks/environments or must be retrained per task; the paper evaluates per-task pruners only, which limits the claimed 'real-time, environment-aware' generality relative to the VLA/generalist-policy framing used to motivate the work in the introduction.

Observation robustness results (Tables 10-11) are mixed: SAG underperforms Full Computation on several perturbations (e.g., simulation distractor/occlusion, hand-occlusion task), which is downplayed in the text as 'small gaps' without deeper analysis of why an adaptive, observation-conditioned pruner would underperform under distribution shift it was ostensibly designed to handle.

At very high pruning rates (97%), performance collapses substantially (avg. success 51%), suggesting the method's real gains are concentrated in a fairly narrow sparsity regime (80-91%) rather than demonstrating robustness to the 'extreme sparsity' framing emphasized in the title/abstract.

Baseline hyperparameters (e.g., cache interval for EfficientVLA, step counts for BAC) appear to be fixed to single values rather than tuned/swept per task, raising some question about whether comparisons are fully optimized for competing methods.

The paper does not report the training cost (wall-clock, GPU-hours) of training the pruner per task, which is relevant for assessing the practicality of the proposed real-time adaptation approach versus fully training-free caching alternatives.
Minor presentation inconsistency between 'prune-then-cache' (contribution list) and 'prune-then-reuse' (used throughout) terminology.
